title: Zanchi: gifts that belong to eternal life and gifts that do not
source_text: VI. Eodem redit quod docet Zanchius libro quarto de Natura Dei cap. 2. quaest. 1. Scilicet ea Dei dona quae nomine gratiae aliquando significantur, vel ad vitam aeternam pertinere, uti sunt fides, spes & charitas, & quae cum iis conjunctae sunt virtutes: vel non pertinere ad vitam aeternam, uti donum linguarum, miraculorum, & alia de quibus Paulus 1 Cor. 12. Quibus similia legere est apud Polanum loco praeallegato.
pass_a_gloss: VI. To the same returns what Zanchius teaches in the fourth book on the Nature of God chap. 2. quest. 1. Namely that those gifts of God which are sometimes signified by the name of grace, either pertain to eternal life, as are faith, hope and charity, and the virtues which are joined with them: or do not pertain to eternal life, as the gift of tongues, of miracles, and others of which Paul 1 Cor. 12. Things similar to which one may read in Polanus in the place previously alleged.
pass_b_english: Thesis VI. Zanchi's teaching in book 4 of On the Nature of God (chapter 2, question 1) comes to the same thing. The gifts of God that are sometimes called grace either belong to eternal life, like faith, hope and love and the virtues joined to them, or do not belong to eternal life, like the gift of tongues, of miracles and the others Paul lists in 1 Corinthians 12.
Similar statements can be read in Polanus at the place already cited.

lemmas.latin: quae cum iis conjunctae sunt virtutes
lemmas.gloss: the virtues which are joined with them

choices.term: gratia gratis data ... gratia gratum faciens
choices.english: grace freely given ... grace that makes pleasing
choices.why: The scholastic pair (Aquinas, Summa theologiae I-II q. 111 a. 1): gifts given for the good of others versus the grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God. Kept literal because the Reformed objections turn on the very words.
